title: Reading Daniel 3 and 6

objectives.can: Read the furnace and the lions' den: lists, repetitions, and loan-words for officials and instruments.

explanation.summary: Daniel 3 and Daniel 6 are the two best-known stories of the Aramaic part of the book. Both are told in a style that repeats itself on purpose: the same lists, the same formulas, the same threat. This lesson reads the opening of Daniel 3 (the golden image) and describes the matching scene in Daniel 6 (the lions' den).

sections.heading: Repetition as a way of telling the story
body: Anyone who reads Daniel 3 notices that the same words come back again and again. The relative phrase דִּי הֲקֵים נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא, 'which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up', appears in 3:2, 3:3 (twice), 3:5 and 3:7. The long list of instruments in 3:5 returns almost word for word in 3:7 and 3:10. The announcement of the penalty in 3:6 returns in 3:11. This is a feature of the style, not a sign of carelessness: the narrator wants the order, the instruments and the penalty to be heard as fixed, so that the disobedience of the three men, when it comes in 3:12, is plain.

When you read a repeated passage, do not skip it. Compare it with the first time. In 3:5 the king's herald speaks to the people ('when you hear'); in 3:7 the narrator tells what happened ('when they heard'); in 3:10 the accusers quote the decree back to the king. The words are the same and the speakers are different, and the verb forms change with the speaker.

sections.heading: The setting: image, dimensions, and who is summoned
body: 3:1 begins with the king's name, then the verb: נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא עֲבַד צְלֵם, 'Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image', a Peal perfect. The next words say what it was made of, and here דִּי joins two nouns with the sense 'of': צְלֵם דִּי דְהַב, 'an image of gold'. There is no verb after דִּי, and that tells you it is 'of'. The measurements follow: רוּמֵהּ אַמִּין שִׁתִּין, 'its height sixty cubits', and פְּתָיֵהּ אַמִּין שִׁת, 'its breadth six cubits'. The nouns רוּמֵהּ and פְּתָיֵהּ are construct nouns with the suffix 'its'.

In 3:2 the king sends to gather his officers: שְׁלַח לְמִכְנַשׁ, 'sent to gather', a Peal perfect followed by a Peal infinitive with לְ, 'to assemble', which gives the purpose. The officials come in a list. In 3:3 the verb is a Hithpaal participle, מִתְכַּנְּשִׁין, 'were gathering' or 'were gathered', a passive-reflexive stem; the participle gives the picture of the scene as it fills up. And וְקָיְמִין, a Peal participle, 'and standing', completes it.

sections.heading: Lists of officials: Persian and Akkadian titles
body: The officials in 3:2 and 3:3 are listed in the determined plural: אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנַיָּא סִגְנַיָּא וּפַחֲוָתָא אֲדַרְגָּזְרַיָּא גְדָבְרַיָּא דְּתָבְרַיָּא תִּפְתָּיֵא, and then וְכֹל שִׁלְטֹנֵי מְדִינָתָא, 'and all the rulers of the provinces'. Most of the names are not native Aramaic words. The lexica trace several to Persian (the titles for the satrap, the counsellor, the treasurer and the judge) and others to the older Babylonian language (סִגְנַיָּא and וּפַחֲוָתָא). The sense of some of them, above all תִּפְתָּיֵא, is uncertain, and English versions differ in the words they choose. A list with the final וְכֹל, 'and all', is how Aramaic wraps up a long list.
The lexica record where the words come from; they do not say when or how the words entered Aramaic, and the grammar leaves that question alone.

sections.heading: The instruments: Greek names in an Aramaic story
body: The sound that gives the signal is the sound of six named instruments, then 'every kind of music': קַרְנָא, מַשְׁרוֹקִיתָא, קַתְרוֹס, סַבְּכָא, פְּסַנְתֵּרִין, סוּמְפֹּנְיָה, וְכֹל זְנֵי זְמָרָא. The first two are Semitic words, 'horn' and 'pipe'. The names for the lyre, the sambuke (a kind of harp), the psalterion and the symphonia are held by the lexica to be Greek words, kithara, sambuke, psalterion and symphonia, taken into Aramaic. The spelling shifts a little between verses (compare סַבְּכָא in 3:5 with שַׂבְּכָא in 3:7).

This is the reason the names are often discussed. Some scholars use the Greek words as evidence for when the book was written; others note that Greek musical words and instruments were known in the Near East earlier than the Greek empire and that the meaning of the names is not always clear. This lesson does not decide the matter. For reading, treat them as a list of six instruments and 'every kind of music'.

sections.heading: The herald, the penalty and the accusation
body: The herald speaks in 3:4: וְכָרוֹזָא קָרֵא בְחָיִל, 'and the herald called aloud', where קָרֵא is a Peal participle used as a narrative verb. His message begins in 3:5 with בְּעִדָּנָא דִּי תִשְׁמְעוּן, 'at the time that you hear'. Here דִּי introduces a clause of time, with the verb in the imperfect. After the list of instruments come two verbs in the imperfect joined by וְ: תִּפְּלוּן וְתִסְגְּדוּן, 'you shall fall down and worship'.

The penalty in 3:6 begins וּמַן דִּי לָא יִפֵּל וְיִסְגֻּד, 'and whoever does not fall down and worship', with the indefinite relative מַן דִּי, 'whoever', and the Hithpeel imperfect יִתְרְמֵא, 'will be thrown', passive in sense, 'into the midst of the furnace of burning fire'. The Chaldeans' complaint in 3:8 uses an idiom: וַאֲכַלוּ קַרְצֵיהוֹן דִּי יְהוּדָיֵא, word for word 'ate their pieces' of the Jews, which the lexica read as 'they accused the Jews'.

In 3:10 the accusers repeat the decree to the king. אַנְתְּ מַלְכָּא שָׂמְתָּ טְעֵם דִּי …, 'you, O king, made a decree that …': the noun טְעֵם is 'decree', and דִּי after it introduces what the decree said. In 3:12 the charge is named: אִיתַי גֻּבְרִין יְהוּדָאיִן דִּי מַנִּיתָ יָתְהוֹן …, 'there are Jewish men whom you appointed …'. Here דִּי is 'whom' and the particle יָתְהוֹן, 'them', repeats it, as Aramaic often does. The last two clauses of the charge are in the negative with participles: לֵאלָהָךְ לָא פָלְחִין, 'they do not serve your god', where the לְ on the noun marks it as the object, and וּלְצֶלֶם דַּהֲבָא … לָא סָגְדִין, 'and the golden image … they do not worship'.

sections.heading: Daniel 6:11–24: the lions' den
body: The second story is described here and is not the passage for the questions. (Verse numbers follow the library's edition, which uses the Hebrew numbering; many English Bibles number this scene one lower.) In 6:11, Daniel hears that the document has been signed, goes to his house, and prays toward Jerusalem: וְזִמְנִין תְּלָתָה בְיוֹמָא הוּא בָּרֵךְ עַל בִּרְכוֹהִי וּמְצַלֵּא וּמוֹדֵא קֳדָם אֱלָהֵהּ, 'and three times a day he was kneeling on his knees and praying and giving thanks before his God'. A run of participles, בָּרֵךְ, וּמְצַלֵּא, וּמוֹדֵא, describes what he used to do, again and again; the narrator uses participles for a habit that went on.

The men who plot catch him: אֱדַיִן גֻּבְרַיָּא אִלֵּךְ הַרְגִּשׁוּ, 'then these men came tumultuously', Haphel perfect. They remind the king of the decree in 6:13: the penalty phrase דִּי כָל אֱנָשׁ דִּי יִבְעֵה … יִתְרְמֵא לְגוֹב אַרְיָוָתָא echoes 3:6 with another punishment. In 6:17 the king says to Daniel אֱלָהָךְ דִּי אַנְתְּ פָּלַח לֵהּ בִּתְדִירָא הוּא יְשֵׁיזְבִנָּךְ, 'your God, whom you serve continually, he will deliver you'. The relative דִּי is repeated by לֵהּ, 'to him', again as in 3:12. The sentence returns in 6:21 as a question: הַיְכִל לְשֵׁיזָבוּתָךְ מִן אַרְיָוָתָא, 'has he been able to deliver you from the lions?' Repetition is again what carries the story from the first scene to the last.

misunderstandings: Skipping a repeated list because 'it was already there'. In these stories the repetition is the style, and small differences, like a different spelling of an instrument or a change of speaker, are worth noticing.

Translating דִּי in every phrase as 'of'. In צְלֵם דִּי דְהַב it is 'of'; in בְּעִדָּנָא דִּי תִשְׁמְעוּן it begins a time clause; in גֻּבְרִין יְהוּדָאיִן דִּי מַנִּיתָ it is 'whom'; in טְעֵם דִּי it introduces the content of the decree.

Treating the Persian or Greek loan-words as if they had been explained by the story. The story does not define them; the lexica's guesses at their meaning are only guesses, and the list of officials is not a precise chart.
Taking the Hithpeel יִתְרְמֵא as 'he throws'. The prefix יִתְ- marks a passive-reflexive stem, and the subject is the one who is thrown.

deeper.heading: Names and the date of the book
body: Both the Persian titles and the Greek instrument names have been used in arguments about when the Aramaic of Daniel was written. The arguments weigh when each word is first attested elsewhere, whether a word could have been borrowed earlier than the evidence shows, and how reliable the spelling in the manuscripts is. The grammar of this lesson does not depend on the answer, and it gives none.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A plain narrative opening: subject, the title in the determined state, a Peal perfect עֲבַד, and the object צְלֵם. The word דִּי here joins 'image' to 'gold' and means 'of'. The measurements come as nouns with suffixes and numerals: 'its height sixty cubits'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: שְׁלַח is the main verb and לְמִכְנַשׁ, a Peal infinitive with לְ, gives the purpose. The seven determined plurals are the list of officials, closed by וְכֹל שִׁלְטֹנֵי מְדִינָתָא, 'and all the rulers of the provinces'. Most of the titles are loan-words.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: that at what time ye hear the sound of the horn, pipe, harp, trigon, psaltery, bagpipe, and all kinds of music, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בְּעִדָּנָא דִּי introduces a time clause: 'at the time that you hear'. The list of instruments is a series of nouns with no conjunction until the last two; the two imperfects תִּפְּלוּן וְתִסְגְּדוּן are the command. The names קַתְרוֹס, פְּסַנְתֵּרִין and סוּמְפֹּנְיָה are the ones the lexica take as Greek.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: and whoso falleth not down and worshippeth shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וּמַן דִּי is 'and whoever'. Two Peal imperfects state the offence in the negative; the Hithpeel יִתְרְמֵא, passive, gives the penalty: he will be thrown into the furnace. The final word is a feminine Peal participle, 'burning'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: There are certain Jews whom thou hast appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: דִּי is a relative, 'whom', and יָתְהוֹן repeats it: 'whom you appointed them'. In the charge, two negated participles, פָלְחִין and סָגְדִין, say the men 'do not serve' and 'do not worship'; the לְ on לֵאלָהָךְ marks the object of the first.

quoted.english: While the word was in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven: 'O king Nebuchadnezzar, to thee it is spoken: the kingdom is departed from thee.

The Chaldeans who accused the Jews
All the peoples, nations and languages
check.explain: The two participles stand after כָּל עַמְמַיָּא אֻמַיָּא וְלִשָּׁנַיָּא, 'all the peoples, nations and languages', who are the subject of both. The three men do not appear until verse 12.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Wherefore at that time certain Chaldeans came near, and brought accusation against the Jews.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: They cut the Jews in pieces
They ate in the house of the Jews
They ate the food of the Jews
check.explain: Word for word it is 'they ate their pieces'; the lexica read it as an idiom for bringing an accusation against someone. The Peal perfect is third person plural, and דִּי here means 'of'.

check.prompt: What does the דִּי after טְעֵם (word 5) do?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Thou, O king, hast made a decree, that every man that shall hear the sound of the horn, pipe, harp, trigon, psaltery, and bagpipe, and all kinds of music, shall fall down and worship the golden image;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It introduces what the decree said: 'that …'
It means 'who' and refers to the king
check.explain: The noun טְעֵם is 'decree'. After שָׂמְתָּ טְעֵם, 'you made a decree', דִּי gives its content: 'that every man who hears … shall fall down and worship'.

check.prompt: What does יָתְהוֹן (word 6) do in דִּי מַנִּיתָ יָתְהוֹן?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: There are certain Jews whom thou hast appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It marks the verb as passive
It is a second subject: 'they appointed'
It repeats the relative as an object: 'whom you appointed them'
It means 'there are' and begins a new clause
check.explain: יָתְהוֹן is the object particle with the suffix 'them'. It points back to the men named in the relative clause, as Aramaic regularly does.

check.prompt: What does the prefix לְ do on לֵאלָהָךְ (word 22) in לֵאלָהָךְ לָא פָלְחִין?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: There are certain Jews whom thou hast appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It marks your god as the object of 'serve'
It turns the participle into a command
It means 'to': they do not go to your god
check.explain: The sense is 'they do not serve your god'. The verb פָלְחִין is a Peal participle, plural, and the לְ marks the object, as in Daniel 6:17 when Daniel is the one brought.

reading.why: The first twelve verses of the story of the golden image: the setting, the two long lists, the herald's decree with its penalty, the repetition of all of it in the accusation, and the charge against the three men. Daniel 6:11–24 is described in the lesson.
